newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mubarak says no to summit, Arafat still to decide.
newsitem.headline: Mubarak says no to summit, Arafat still to decide.

text.p: Preparations for a Middle East summit in Washington stumbled ahead on Monday, with Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak declining to attend and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat refusing to commit himself.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and King Hussein of Jordan left for the meeting, called by U.S. President Bill Clinton to help end five days of clashes in which 55 Palestinians and 14 Israelis died.

But Mubarak, whose country in 1979 became the first Arab nation to make peace with Israel and has mediated in Arab-Israeli peace talks since, appeared to doubt the summit would push Israel into advancing the peace process with the Palestinians.

Arafat, who met Mubarak on Monday to coordinate positions on the summit, left Cairo for a late evening meeting with European Union ministers in Luxembourg refusing to say whether he would attend the Washington summit.
Netanyahu told reporters aboard his plane to Washington that Palestinians and Israelis should begin non-stop negotiations on Israeli troop redeployment in Hebron.
Israeli troops should already have redeployed in the West Bank town under a previous deal between the two sides but the Jewish state has delayed citing security concerns.

The latest violence between Palestinians and Israelis -- the worst since the two sides began peace talks -- began when Israel opened a controversial tunnel near the Aqsa mosque in Jerusalem, Islam's third holiest site.
Arafat and Mubarak want Israel to close the tunnel but Netanyahu repeated enroute to the United States that it would stay open and would not be on the summit's agenda.

Mubarak told his party newspaper in an interview published on Monday he was concerned "the situation can explode again, as long as the agreements and treaties are not implemented" and warned of a new Palestinian uprising.
The United States tried to play down Mubarak's decision not to attend the summit, with White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry saying Mubarak had a "scheduling conflict".
But Egyptian officials said Mubarak was due to open a new line of the Cairo underground on Tuesday and made clear he did not believe the summit would move Netanyahu from his hardline positions.
Egyptian Information Minister Safwat el-Sherif confirmed in an interview with the Arabic service of the British Broadcasting Corporation that Mubarak would not attend the Washington summit.

Sherif said Egypt had wanted the summit to be better prepared and referred to a meeting in July between Mubarak and Netanyahu, saying the Israeli prime minister had not carried out any of the promises he had made to Mubarak.

Earlier Osama el-Baz, Mubarak's adviser, told reporters after Arafat's departure that the Palestinian leader "will probably go" to Washington but the Palestinian ambassador to Cairo said Arafat would decide later on Monday.

"Our only concern is how best to serve the cause of peace, to produce tangible and concrete results on the ground and revive the hope in the minds and hearts of the people in the region that the peace process is still alive," Baz said.

Arafat's meeting in Luxembourg with the European troika -- made up of Ireland, Italy and the Netherlands -- was widely seen as an attempt to bolster the European role in the peace talks after the U.S. shut it out of the summit.

"Tonight's meeting of the European troika with President (Yasser) Arafat in Luxembourg...underlines the role of Europe in the Middle East peace process, especially since it is being held before the Washington summit," Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told Reuters.
"We will also be asking President Arafat tonight for an assurance of the will on both sides to proceed along the path of peace," Dini said.
